title: Natural, made and tested: choosing materials like a scientist
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 Chemistry: Unit 3.1 'Natural and made materials', Unit 3.2 'Properties of materials', Unit 3.3 'Using the right material' and Unit 3.4 'Testing materials'. No textbook needed.
summary: Last year your child learned that every object is made of a material. Now they find out which materials are natural and which people make, and follow the journeys that turn cotton into cloth, sand into glass and clay into bricks. They learn the scientist's property words (rigid, flexible, absorbent, waterproof, transparent), sort with a Venn diagram, and run real fair tests with measurements, a table and a block graph. They meet the cloudy liquid that became one of the strongest fibres ever made, and they bury materials to see which ones the Earth can take back.
builds_on: Class 1: object and material; hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, stretchy, see-through, waterproof; simple tests; where materials come from. Next: Changing materials (Class 2) heats, cools and burns them; Class 3 adds transparent, translucent and opaque, magnetic metals and branching keys; Making things (Classes 3–5) follows materials into houses, paper and cloth.
subconcepts: raw materials and how people change them
a material's journey: cotton to cloth, sand to glass, clay to brick, oil to plastic
property words: rigid, flexible, waterproof, absorbent, transparent, strong
a material's properties decide its uses
a fair test: change one thing, keep the rest the same, measure
recording results in a table and a block graph
the cost of a material to the Earth
goals: By the end your child can sort materials into natural and made, and explain that made materials are changed from natural ones.
By the end your child can tell the journey of three materials from raw material to object.
By the end your child can use the words rigid, flexible, absorbent, waterproof and transparent correctly.
By the end your child can plan and carry out a fair test, saying what they changed, what they kept the same and what they measured.
By the end your child can record results in a table and a block graph and say what the results show.
By the end your child can explain what biodegradable means and why it matters which materials we choose.
words: a material found in nature: wood, wool, cotton, stone, clay
a material people make by changing natural ones: glass, plastic, steel, paper, brick
the natural stuff a made material starts from, like sand for glass
stiff; it keeps its shape and does not bend
it soaks up water, like a sponge or towel
it does not let water through
you can see clearly through it
a test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same
a chart of blocks or bars that shows numbers so you can compare them
two overlapping circles for sorting things that can belong to both groups
it can be broken down by tiny living things into soil and air

days.title: Natural or made?
days.goal: Recall last year's materials and split them into natural and made.

steps.title: Remember the crow?
steps.do: Ask: 'Last year a crow built a nest of wire, twigs, coir, cotton and wool. What is the difference between an object and a material?' (the object is the thing, the material is the stuff). 'Why did the crow use wire on the outside?' (strong and bendy). Then hand your child a steel spoon and a wooden spoon: 'Same object, two materials. Which one would you stir hot dal with, and why?' (wood, because steel gets hot).

steps.title: Natural or made hunt
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Go round the house and outside. Your child finds 6 natural materials (a stone, a leaf, a twig, wool, a shell, soil or clay) and 6 made materials (a plastic bucket, a glass bottle, a steel plate, a paper bag, a brick, a nylon rope). Put them in two heaps on a mat. Ask about each one: 'Did a person change this from something else?'

steps.title: The tricky ones
steps.do: Hold up a cotton kurta. Ask: 'Natural or made?' Let your child argue. The answer: cotton is a natural material, but the cloth was made by people who spun and wove it. Then a wooden chair (natural wood, shaped by people), paper (made, from wood), a brick (made, from clay). Say: 'Every made material started as a natural one. People changed it.' Write the rule on a card for the wall.

need: a steel spoon and a wooden spoon

days.title: A material's journey
days.goal: Follow raw materials as people change them, and start the burial test.

steps.title: Journey chains
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Your child draws four journey chains with arrows, one box per step, while you tell each one. Cotton: cotton plant → fluffy bolls picked → spun into thread → woven into cloth → kurta. Sand: sand from a river or beach → melted in a furnace hotter than any kitchen fire → blown or moulded → glass bottle. Clay: clay dug from the ground → mixed with water and shaped → dried and baked in a kiln → brick. Oil: oil pumped from deep underground → changed in a factory into tiny beads → melted and moulded → plastic bucket. Ask: 'Which journey needs the most fire?'

steps.title: The steel the world wanted
steps.do: Tell voice v1: more than 2,000 years ago, ironworkers in South India melted iron with plant material in small clay pots and made a steel the rest of the world wanted, called wootz. Traders carried it across the sea to make the famous 'Damascus' swords. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Start the burial test
steps.do: Set up Experiment e3. Bury, in a pot of damp garden soil, small labelled pieces of: a banana peel, a cotton rag, a piece of newspaper, a plastic bag, a piece of foil and a leaf. Push a lolly stick next to each. Ask your child to predict which will be gone in two weeks. Write the predictions down and keep the soil damp.

need: banana peel, cotton rag, newspaper, plastic bag, foil, a leaf

days.title: The scientist's property words
days.goal: Learn the precise words for properties, and meet the cloudy liquid.

steps.title: Property stations
steps.do: Set up five stations on a table, each with three things and a label. RIGID or FLEXIBLE: a steel ruler, a plastic ruler, a sheet of paper. ABSORBENT or not: a sponge, a steel plate, a cotton cloth (drip water on each). WATERPROOF or not: a plastic bag, newspaper, foil. TRANSPARENT or not: a clear bottle, a cardboard box, butter paper. STRONG or WEAK: a jute string, a cotton thread, a strand of hair (pull gently). Your child visits each station, tests, and says a sentence with the new word: 'The sponge is absorbent.'

steps.title: Story: The Cloudy Liquid
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain. Ask: 'Why did the other scientists think the liquid was no good?' (it was cloudy and thin, not clear and syrupy like the good ones). 'How did Stephanie find out what it could do?' (she tested it: they spun it into a fibre). Then tell voice v2 and ask its question.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Read each item aloud. In the written questions, push for a reason: 'because…'

need: a dropper or spoon and water

days.title: The thirsty test
days.goal: Run a fair test with measuring, a table and a block graph.

steps.title: What makes a test fair?
steps.do: Ask: 'If I race you, but I start halfway down the road, is it fair?' (no). 'In a science test, what must be the same?' Explain: we change ONE thing (the material) and keep everything else the same (the size of the piece, the amount of water, the time). We MEASURE what happens. Ask: 'Can we answer "which is the prettiest towel?" with a test?' (no, people disagree). 'What about "which towel soaks up most water?"' (yes, we can measure it).

steps.title: Which material is most absorbent?
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child dips same-sized squares of five materials into water for 10 seconds, lets each drip for 5 seconds, then squeezes it out into a small cup and counts how many spoons of water come out. Record in the table on Worksheet ws1's back or a sheet: material, spoons of water.

steps.title: Make a block graph
steps.do: On squared paper, your child colours one square for each spoon of water, one column per material. Ask: 'Which column is tallest? Which material is most absorbent? Which would you choose for a towel, and which for a raincoat?' (most absorbent for the towel, least absorbent for the raincoat).

need: 5 squares (10 cm) of: cotton cloth, paper towel, newspaper, plastic sheet, woollen cloth or sponge cloth
a teaspoon and a small cup

days.title: The strongest bag
days.goal: Test strength fairly and learn that one result is not enough.

steps.title: Which paper makes the strongest bag?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Make three small bags of the same size, the same way, from three papers: newspaper, printer paper and a brown paper bag or kraft paper. Hang each by a string handle from a door knob and add coins one by one until it tears. Count the coins. Do it twice for each paper if you have enough paper. Ask: 'Why did we make the bags the same size?'

steps.title: Why test twice?
steps.do: If the two tries gave different numbers, ask: 'Why might that be?' (a bag was glued badly, a coin was dropped hard). Say: 'Scientists repeat tests so one accident doesn't fool them.' Ask: 'What else could change how strong a bag is, besides the paper?' (the shape, the glue, how the handle is fixed, folding the paper double).

steps.title: Check the burial test
steps.do: Gently dig up the banana peel in Experiment e3 with a spoon and look: has it changed colour? Is it soft? Push it back, re-bury and water the soil a little. Don't dig up the others yet.

prep.task: Collect 50 one-rupee coins or marbles of the same size

days.title: Sorting and choosing
days.goal: Sort with a Venn diagram and match materials to jobs.

steps.title: Floor Venn diagram
steps.do: Lay two hoops or two dupattas in overlapping circles on the floor. Label one FLEXIBLE and one WATERPROOF. Your child places 10 objects: a plastic bag (both, in the middle), a steel plate (waterproof but not flexible), a cotton hanky (flexible, not waterproof), a rubber glove (both), a wooden block (neither, outside both circles), a sheet of paper, a foil sheet, a glass bottle, a woollen sock, a balloon. Ask: 'What does it mean to be in the middle? What about outside both circles?'

steps.title: Design challenges
steps.do: Ask your child to choose materials for: a raincoat for a cat (waterproof, flexible, light), a window for a submarine (transparent, very strong, waterproof), a mop (absorbent, flexible), a bridge for ants across a bucket (rigid, light, strong). For each, they must name the properties first, then the material. There are several good answers.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. For the Venn question, let your child draw the two circles first.

days.title: What can the Earth take back?
days.goal: Dig up the burial test and think about materials that don't go back.

steps.title: Dig it up
steps.do: Dig up everything in Experiment e3 on a newspaper. Compare with the predictions. Your child sorts the pieces: CHANGED A LOT (banana peel, leaf), CHANGED A LITTLE (newspaper, cotton), NOT CHANGED (plastic, foil). Say the word biodegradable: broken down by tiny living things, bacteria and fungi, back into soil and air. Ask: 'Which made materials did the Earth take back? Which did it not?'

steps.title: The compost question
steps.do: Tell voice v3. Some plastics now say 'compostable' on the packet. Ask: 'How could we test if a packet that says compostable really is?' (bury it like our test, and check after weeks or months). 'Who should test it: the company or someone else? Why?'

steps.title: Material Journey board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1. Each player is a material on its journey from the Earth and back again. Read each square aloud and say whether it helps or slows the material.

need: the printed board, a die and counters

days.title: The bag project, and teach it back
days.goal: Use a fair test to choose the best vegetable bag, and explain everything.

steps.title: Project: the best vegetable bag
steps.do: Do the project. Your child tests three cloth or paper bags for carrying vegetables home: strength (how many potatoes before it tears or stretches badly), waterproof (one spoon of water), and whether it can be washed and reused. They fill in a small table and choose a winner, with reasons.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. The last questions have no single answer; ask your child to give reasons and to say how they would test their idea.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child explains to a family member: natural and made materials (with a journey), the five property words, how to make a test fair, what the burial test showed, and the cloudy-liquid story. Then ask the check questions.

need: 3 bags: a cloth bag, a paper bag, a jute or plastic bag

A sponge soaks up water. It is…
A steel ruler does not bend. It is…
You can see clearly through a window because glass is ____.
A raincoat keeps water out because it is ____.
A kurta is made of cotton. Is it natural or made? Explain your answer.
Why would a towel made of plastic be a bad towel?
Ravi tests which cloth soaks up most water. Which must he keep the same?
Which question can you answer with a test?
opts: Which towel soaks up most water?

sections.p: In a fair test we change only ____ thing.
Copy your thirsty-test results here.
Flexible, waterproof, both or neither?
Match the job to the best material.
Your bag test gave 12 coins one time and 20 coins the next. What would you do, and why?
Design a raincoat for a cat. Which properties does it need? Which material would you pick?
In the burial test, which piece changed least?
Biodegradable means…
opts: it can be broken down by tiny living things
it is made in a factory

sections.p: Stephanie's liquid looked cloudy. What did the test show?
opts: it made a very strong fibre

sections.p: Wootz was a famous ____ made in South India long ago.
Which can the Earth take back quickly, and which slowly or hardly at all?
Match the material to how it is made.
Stephanie's liquid looked wrong, but turned out to be amazing. Can you always tell what a material can do by looking at it? How do you find out?
Plastic is waterproof, cheap and strong, and it lasts for a very long time. Is lasting a long time good or bad? When?
Invent a test to find out whether a 'compostable' cup really breaks down. What will you change, keep the same and look for?

experiments.title: The thirsty test: which material is most absorbent?
experiments.question: Which material soaks up the most water?
need: 5 squares, 10 cm by 10 cm, of cotton cloth, paper towel, newspaper, plastic sheet and woollen cloth or a sponge cloth
steps: Dip the first square in the bowl for 10 seconds.
Lift it and let it drip over the bowl for 5 seconds.
Squeeze it out into the small cup.
Count how many teaspoons of water you can scoop from the cup.
Empty the cup and repeat for each material.
Write each result in a table, then draw a block graph.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to put the five squares in order from 'will soak up most' to 'will soak up least' before you start.
experiments.observe: The number of spoons from each material. Plastic gives almost none; paper towel and cotton give the most.
experiments.why: Absorbent materials are made of tiny fibres with spaces between them. Water creeps into the spaces and is held there, like water in a sponge's holes. Plastic has no spaces, so water just runs off. Keeping the size, dipping time and drip time the same makes the test fair, so the material is the only thing that changes.
experiments.safety: Wipe up spills so nobody slips.

experiments.title: Which paper makes the strongest bag?
experiments.question: Which kind of paper makes the strongest bag?
need: newspaper, printer paper and brown kraft paper
steps: Make three bags the same size (about 15 cm by 10 cm) and the same way, one from each paper.
Fix a string handle to each in the same way.
Hang the first bag from the door knob.
Drop in coins one at a time, gently, counting, until the bag tears.
Write down the number of coins.
Repeat with the other bags. If you can, make a second set and test again.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which bag will hold the most coins? How many?'
experiments.observe: How many coins each bag holds before tearing, and where it tears (often at the handle or the glued edge).
experiments.why: Paper is a mat of tangled plant fibres. Brown kraft paper has long, strong fibres pressed tightly together, so it holds more. Newspaper has short fibres and is thin. A test repeated gives more reliable results: if one bag tore early because of a bad glue joint, the second try shows it.
experiments.safety: Drop coins gently and keep feet clear.

experiments.title: The burial test
experiments.question: Which materials can the soil break down?
need: a large pot or tub of damp garden soil
small pieces of banana peel, cotton rag, newspaper, plastic bag, foil and a leaf
steps: Bury each piece about 5 cm deep in a different part of the pot.
Mark each with a labelled lolly stick.
Keep the soil damp, not soaking, in a shady place.
On Day 5, check only the banana peel.
On Day 7 (about two weeks later if you can wait), dig everything up and compare.
experiments.predict: Write your child's prediction for each piece: gone, changed, or the same.
experiments.observe: The banana peel and leaf turn brown, soft and broken; the newspaper and cotton go soft and start to fall apart; the plastic and foil look almost the same.
experiments.why: Bacteria, fungi and small animals like worms eat materials that came from living things recently: peel, leaves, paper and cotton. These are biodegradable. Most plastics are made of long chains that these tiny living things cannot easily eat, so they stay for a very long time and break only into smaller pieces. Foil is a metal and does not rot at all.
experiments.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Use garden soil, not soil from a drain or dump.

activities.title: Natural or made hunt
steps: Find 6 natural materials and 6 made materials.
Put them in two heaps.
For each, ask: did a person change this from something else?
activities.outcome: Two heaps, and a first feeling for 'natural' and 'made'.

activities.title: Journey chains
steps: Draw a box for each step of a material's journey.
Join the boxes with arrows.
Do cotton, sand, clay and oil.
activities.outcome: Four journey chains for the wall.

activities.title: Floor Venn diagram
steps: Overlap two circles on the floor.
Label them FLEXIBLE and WATERPROOF.
Place each object: one circle, the middle, or outside.
activities.outcome: Your child understands that a thing can belong to two groups, one, or none.

project.title: The best vegetable bag
steps: Get three bags: a cloth bag, a paper bag, and a jute or plastic bag.
Decide what a good vegetable bag needs: strong, doesn't leak when vegetables are wet, can be reused.
Test strength: add potatoes one at a time and count how many before it tears or stretches badly.
Test waterproofness: pour one spoon of water inside and look underneath.
Fill in a table and choose a winner, with reasons.
Talk about how many times each bag could be used again.
project.outcome: A small table of results and a reasoned choice of the best bag, which the family then uses.

game.title: Material Journey
rules: Each player chooses to be a material: cotton, sand, clay or wood.
Start at THE EARTH. Roll the die and move.
Read the square aloud. Do what it says.
The first to reach BACK TO THE EARTH wins, but you must explain one property of your material to finish.
squares: Dug or picked by hand: move on 1
Carried on a truck: roll again
A furnace: go forward 2 (glass and brick only; others back 1)
Tested: is it strong? Say a property
Thrown in a river: miss a turn
Eaten by bacteria (cotton and wood only: forward 2)

big: If every made material started as a natural one, is anything really 'unnatural'?
Is a material that lasts for ever a good thing or a problem?
Can you tell what something can do just by looking at it?
Who should test whether a company's product does what it says?
Should we choose the cheapest material, the strongest, or the kindest to the Earth?

challenge.q: People say paper bags are always better for the Earth than plastic bags. Is that true?
challenge.hint: It depends on how many times a bag is used. A study for England's Environment Agency (2011) found that making a paper bag uses more energy than a thin plastic one, so a paper bag must be reused a few times to do better, and a cotton bag many times more. But paper rots and thin plastic doesn't. Ask: what matters more, how it is made or where it ends up?

challenge.q: Some packets say 'biodegradable'. Does that mean they will vanish in your garden?
challenge.hint: Not always. Some only break down in very hot factory compost. A large study in Britain in 2022 found that many plastics labelled 'home compostable' had not fully broken down in people's home compost heaps. Ask: what should a label have to prove?

challenge.q: Is glass a natural or a made material?
challenge.hint: People make glass by melting sand. But glass also forms naturally: obsidian is glass made by volcanoes, and lightning hitting sand can make glass tubes. So the line between natural and made is fuzzier than it looks.

perspectives.view: Before a kurta reaches a shop, a farmer grew the cotton, often in hard heat, and was paid only a small part of what the kurta costs. Ask: who in the journey of a material gets the most money, and who does the most work?
To a worm, a banana peel is dinner and a plastic bag is a wall. Ask: if worms could choose our materials, what would they choose?
Engineers test materials until they break, on purpose, so the real bridge never does. Ask: why is breaking things sometimes the most careful thing to do?

voices.who: The wootz steel makers of ancient South India and Sri Lanka
voices.idea: More than 2,000 years ago, ironworkers in South India and Sri Lanka melted iron with plant material inside small sealed clay pots (crucibles) to make a high-quality steel. It was traded across the Arabian Sea and forged in the Middle East into famous 'Damascus' blades with wavy patterns.
voices.then: Travellers and traders admired the steel; for a long time European smiths could not copy it.
voices.now: Archaeologists have found crucible steel sites in South India and Sri Lanka, and metallurgists have studied the blades and accept their Indian and Sri Lankan origin. The makers' names are lost, and the skill died out by the 1800s.
voices.ask: The makers of wootz wrote no books, but their steel travelled the world. How do we know what people knew, if they didn't write it down?

voices.who: Stephanie Kwolek (1923–2014) and Charles Smullen, DuPont, USA
voices.idea: In 1964–65, Kwolek was looking for a light, strong fibre. She made a polymer liquid that was cloudy and thin, when good ones were usually clear and thick. Instead of throwing it away, she asked Smullen, who ran the spinning machine, to spin it. The fibre turned out, for its weight, far stronger than steel. It became Kevlar, used in protective vests, gloves and ropes.
voices.then: Smullen at first did not want to spin it, worried it would clog the machine. Once tested, the fibre amazed the company.
voices.now: Kwolek is honoured as a great inventor and was inducted into the US National Inventors Hall of Fame. Smullen's part is less often told.
voices.ask: What would have happened if Stephanie had judged the liquid by how it looked? Why was Charles's help needed too?

voices.who: Danielle Purkiss and colleagues, University College London, 'The Big Compost Experiment' (2022)
voices.idea: Thousands of people in Britain tested packaging labelled 'compostable' or 'home compostable' in their own compost heaps. Many of the items had not fully broken down when people checked.
voices.then: Companies selling the packaging said it was tested under standard conditions; the scientists said home compost heaps are often cooler and different from test conditions.
voices.now: Scientists are still arguing about which labels are trustworthy and how they should be tested. Many agree that 'compostable' plastic needs the right conditions, which most homes don't have.
voices.ask: The company tested its packet, and ordinary people tested it too, and they got different answers. Whose test would you trust more, and why?

story.title: The Cloudy Liquid
text: I was born in a glass bottle on a hot afternoon in 1965, in a laboratory in Delaware, in America. My mother was a chemist called Stephanie Kwolek. That is how I think of her, anyway, though she would have laughed at being called the mother of a bottle of liquid.

Stephanie was looking for something that did not exist yet. Her company wanted a new fibre for car tyres: a thread lighter than steel wire, but just as strong, so cars could be lighter and use less fuel. For months she had been mixing long chain-like molecules into liquids and sending them to be spun into threads. Most of the threads were weak. Some fell apart. None was the one.

I was not what anyone expected. A good liquid for spinning, everybody knew, was clear and thick, like honey. I was thin and runny, like buttermilk. And I was cloudy. When Stephanie stirred me, I shimmered, opal-grey, as if there were clouds moving inside me.
A chemist walking past the bench looked over her shoulder. 'That's spoiled,' he said. 'You've got bits of something stuck in it. Throw it out and start again.'
Stephanie held me up to the window. The light came through me, broken into soft shining streaks. She did not throw me out.

Instead, she did something careful. She filtered me, pouring me slowly through a fine filter to catch any bits of dirt. If I were cloudy because of rubbish, the rubbish would stay in the filter and I would come out clear. I went through. Nothing was left behind. I came out just as cloudy as before.
So the cloudiness was not dirt. It was me. It was the way my long molecules had lined up together, side by side, like matchsticks in a box all pointing the same way.

The next step was the spinneret: a machine with a metal plate full of tiny holes, which pushed liquid through to make threads, like the holes of a sev maker pushing out dough. It was run by a man called Charles Smullen. Stephanie carried me to him.
Charles looked at me and shook his head. 'I'm not putting that in my machine,' he said. 'It's cloudy. It's got particles in it. It'll block all the holes and I'll spend a week cleaning it.'
Stephanie told him about the filter. She asked again. He said no again. She asked a third time, and kept asking, politely and stubbornly, for days. I sat in my bottle on her bench and waited.
At last Charles sighed and said, 'All right. Once.'

He poured me into the machine. I remember the squeeze of the tiny holes, the long fall into the bath below, and the strange feeling of becoming something new: not a liquid any more, but a thread, fine and golden-yellow, wound round and round a spool.

Then they tested me. They pulled me in a machine that measures how hard you must pull before a thread snaps. They pulled, and pulled, and I did not snap. They checked the machine to see if it was broken. It wasn't. They tested me again. For my weight, I was about five times stronger than steel. And I was stiff, so stiff that I hardly stretched at all.

Stephanie and her colleagues kept working on me and my cousins, and the family of threads that grew from me became known as Kevlar. Today it is woven into vests that protect police officers and soldiers, into gloves that keep cooks' and glassworkers' fingers safe from sharp edges, into ropes that hold ships, and into the skins of spacecraft. Many people are alive because of it.

But I like to remember the bottle on the bench, and the window, and the cloudy light. Everybody who looked at me saw something wrong. Only one person asked what I could do. And only one more person, after saying no three times, was willing to find out.
story.epiphany: You cannot know a material's properties by looking; you find out by testing. The cloudy, runny liquid looked 'wrong' against everyone's rule, but when it was filtered (a test), and then spun and pulled (more tests), it proved to be one of the strongest fibres ever made. The turn is the pulling machine: the material speaks for itself. Underneath: a woman scientist trusting her own careful observation, and a technician whose help made the discovery possible.
ask: Why did people think the liquid was spoiled?
What did Stephanie do to check whether the cloudiness was dirt? What did it show?
Why did Charles say no? Was he being silly or careful?
How did they find out how strong the thread was?
Have you ever judged something by how it looked and been wrong?

ideas.idea: Every 'made' material began as a natural one.
ideas.more: Glass is melted sand, steel is changed rock, plastic is changed oil, paper is mashed wood. People don't make materials from nothing; they transform what the Earth gives.

ideas.idea: You find out what a material can do by testing it fairly, not by how it looks.
ideas.more: Change one thing, keep the rest the same, measure, repeat. The cloudy liquid looked useless and was one of the strongest fibres ever made.

ideas.idea: Some materials the Earth can take back, and some it can't, for a very long time.
ideas.more: Bacteria and fungi recycle peel, leaves, cotton and paper. Most plastics, glass and metals stay. Choosing a material also chooses where it ends up.

unknowns: Nobody knows for sure how the old Indian and Sri Lankan smiths controlled every step of wootz steel; metallurgists have made similar steel, but whether they have matched every secret is still argued about.
How long do the tiny broken bits of plastic stay in soil and sea, and what do they do to living things? Scientists are still measuring.
What undiscovered materials are waiting in mixtures nobody has tried yet? Chemists find new ones every year, and many good ones, like Kevlar, were surprises.

check.q: Name two natural and two made materials.
check.a: Natural: wood, wool, cotton, stone, clay. Made: glass, plastic, steel, paper, brick.

check.q: Tell the journey of glass or brick.
check.a: Glass: sand is melted in a very hot furnace and shaped. Brick: clay is dug, shaped, dried and baked in a kiln.

check.q: What does absorbent mean? Which material in our test was most absorbent?
check.a: It soaks up water. Usually the paper towel or cotton.

check.q: How did we make the thirsty test fair?
check.a: Same size pieces, same dipping time, same dripping time; only the material changed.

check.q: Why do scientists repeat a test?
check.a: So one mistake or accident doesn't fool them; repeated results are more reliable.

check.q: What happened to the plastic and the banana peel in the burial test? Why?
check.a: The peel rotted because tiny living things ate it (biodegradable); the plastic hardly changed because they can't eat it easily.

check.q: How did Stephanie Kwolek find out her cloudy liquid was special?
check.a: She tested it: filtered it, then had it spun into a thread and pulled, and it was very strong.
